This document outlines a protocol for a Cochrane Review aimed at evaluating interventions to improve insulin resistance for the prevention of atypical endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer. 2. The primary objective is to assess the safety and effectiveness of these interventions in reducing the risk of atypical endometrial hyperplasia, endometrial cancer, or both. 3. Endometrial cancer, which arises from abnormal growth of the uterine lining (endometrium), is the most common cancer affecting the female reproductive system in developed countries. 4. Endometrial hyperplasia, a thickening of the uterine lining, can progress to endometrial cancer if left untreated. 5. Globally, endometrial cancer affects approximately 382,000 women annually, with over 9,000 cases reported in the UK alone. 6. The incidence of endometrial cancer has increased by 57% in the UK since the early 1990s, with similar trends observed worldwide. 7. Most women diagnosed with endometrial cancer are postmenopausal, with 93% of cases in the UK occurring in women over the age of 50. 8. However, there is a growing number of younger, premenopausal women being diagnosed with the disease. 9. The increase in incidence is primarily attributed to low-grade Type 1 endometrial cancers, which are largely driven by an excess of unopposed estrogen. 10. Other risk factors for endometrial cancer include advancing age, insulin resistance, and diabetes, with obesity being the common link among these factors. 11. The global prevalence of obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m²) has doubled in the last 30 years, and endometrial cancer has the strongest association with obesity among the 20 most common tumor types. 12. A 5 kg/m² increase in BMI is associated with a 60% increase in endometrial cancer risk, and women with a BMI of 42 kg/m² have a nine-fold higher risk compared to those with a BMI of 22 kg/m². 13. Theories linking obesity to endometrial cancer include an excess of pro-growth factors like estrogen, increased inflammation, and insulin resistance. 14. Insulin resistance occurs when target tissues such as the liver, skeletal muscle, and fat do not respond appropriately to insulin, leading to impaired glucose metabolism. 15. If the pancreas cannot produce sufficient compensatory insulin, chronic hyperglycemia (high blood glucose) and hyperinsulinemia (high insulin levels) can result, eventually leading to Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). 16. In obese individuals, dysregulation of signaling proteins like tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and adiponectin contributes to chronic inflammation and insulin resistance. 17. Prolonged high insulin levels have been associated with an increased incidence of various cancers, including colorectal, hepatic, pancreatic, breast, and endometrial cancers. 18. Women with T2DM have a two-fold increased risk of developing endometrial cancer compared to women without diabetes. 19. While most obese women are insulin resistant, insulin resistance and diabetes are independent risk factors for endometrial cancer. 20. Insulin resistance alone continues to increase the risk of endometrial cancer, even after adjusting for the effects of obesity. 21. Insulin and its related protein, insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), play critical roles in promoting cell proliferation, differentiation, and metabolic activity in the normal endometrium. 22. These effects are mediated through activation of growth signaling pathways such as PI3K/AKT/mTOR and MAPK, which are implicated in endometrial cancer development. 23. Elevated insulin and IGF-1 levels are associated with increased endometrial growth, raising the risk of abnormal endometrial cells and eventual cancer formation. 24. Increased expression of insulin and IGF-1 receptors, along with overactivation of associated growth signaling pathways, has been observed in endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer. 25. Early-stage endometrial cancer is typically treated surgically by removing the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. 26. In cases of aggressive or advanced disease, surgery is often followed by radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or both. 27. For women of childbearing potential, these treatments result in infertility, which can be devastating for those who have not completed their families. 28. Most women with endometrial cancer are diagnosed at an early stage (FIGO stage I or II), where the disease is curable. 29. However, obesity can complicate surgery, increasing the risk of complications and healthcare costs. 30. Preventive interventions for endometrial cancer would provide significant benefits for both patients and healthcare systems. 31. In high-risk women with a familial predisposition to endometrial cancer (e.g., Lynch Syndrome), early identification allows for genetic follow-up and access to cancer surveillance programs. 32. Risk-reducing surgery, such as hysterectomy and removal of tubes and ovaries after family completion, is an established method of preventing endometrial cancer in these women. 33. Some women are diagnosed with endometrial hyperplasia, a precursor lesion that can progress to cancer if untreated, with the highest risk seen in atypical endometrial hyperplasia. 34. Atypical hyperplasia in women who have completed their families is treated surgically with a hysterectomy, removing the uterus and cervix. 35. Women wishing to retain fertility or those unfit for surgery can be treated with a progesterone-releasing hormone coil (e.g., Mirena), oral progestogens, and weight loss interventions. 36. Oral progestogens have side effects such as headaches, mood changes, and acne, and long-term use increases the risk of venous blood clots and breast cancer. 37. Disease regression rates of up to 86% have been reported in atypical endometrial hyperplasia, but significant disease recurrences are also recognized. 38. Prevention strategies in the general population focus on targeting established risk factors, such as manipulating sex hormones through oral, injectable, or intrauterine progestins. 39. The combined oral contraceptive pill is associated with a reduction in lifetime endometrial cancer risk. 40. In obese women with a BMI > 35 kg/m², the risks of thromboembolic events outweigh the potential benefits of hormonal interventions. 41. Another potential intervention is improving insulin resistance in women at increased risk, such as those with diabetes or obesity. 42. Women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) have a three-fold increased risk of developing endometrial cancer, likely driven by insulin resistance and unopposed estrogen. 43. Metformin and other drugs that improve insulin sensitivity have been proposed as potential interventions for endometrial cancer prevention. 44. Metformin, widely used for T2DM, PCOS, infertility, obesity, and hirsutism, reduces cancer growth by decreasing glucose production in the liver and activating AMPK, which inhibits cancer proliferation pathways. 45. Epidemiological studies suggest that diabetic patients taking metformin have a lower cancer burden compared to those treated with other agents. 46. A meta-analysis of 11 studies found that metformin use was associated with a 13% reduction in endometrial cancer risk in women with diabetes. 47. However, conflicting evidence exists, with some studies finding no significant association between metformin use and endometrial cancer risk. 48. Discrepancies in study findings may be due to differences in study design, sample size, and treatment duration. 49. Public health interventions that reduce obesity prevalence could significantly decrease endometrial cancer incidence. 50. Intentional weight loss, particularly in obese women, has been reported to lower endometrial cancer risk, consistent with findings from bariatric surgery studies. 51. Improvements in insulin resistance, as measured by HOMA-IR, are observed shortly after bariatric surgery, even before significant weight loss occurs. 52. Sustained weight loss is associated with improvements in insulin resistance and blood sugar control, suggesting that both non-pharmacological and surgical interventions may favorably impact insulin resistance. 53. The burden of endometrial cancer is increasing in developed countries and is expected to rise in lower-income countries as obesity becomes more prevalent. 54. Prevention strategies must target the key mechanisms driving endometrial cancer development, with insulin resistance being a critical area for further investigation. 55. This review will evaluate existing evidence and identify whether well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed to assess the feasibility, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness of interventions targeting insulin resistance for endometrial cancer prevention.
